sections.text:
Paul compares himself to a mother. When he first came to Thessalonica, he says, “we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.” It is a tender picture from a man who had to leave this young church in a hurry, and who writes to them now with feeling.

He gives thanks for their faith under pressure and recalls his time with them. When Timothy brings a good report, Paul is relieved. He encourages them to live holy lives and to keep working quietly.

Then he turns to a grief the church is carrying: some believers have died. Paul writes so that they will not grieve like people with no hope. When the Lord returns, “The dead in Christ will rise first,” and all will be with him forever. No one knows when that day will come, so they are told, “let’s watch and be sober.”

Thessalonica was the chief city of Macedonia. Paul founded the church there on his second journey (Acts 17) and wrote from Corinth around the year 50 or 51. It is among the earliest of his letters, and of the whole New Testament.

The passage about being caught up to meet the Lord (4:17) is the main basis for the teaching called the rapture. Some Christians expect believers to be taken before a period of great trouble. Many others read it as part of the single return of Christ, with believers going out to welcome him. Both sides take the passage seriously, and both start from the same comfort the letter offers: that those who have died are not lost.

This may be the earliest letter in the New Testament, and it begins with gratitude. Paul, Silvanus and Timothy write to the assembly of the Thessalonians. They always give thanks for them, remembering “your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ”.

They know the Thessalonians are chosen, because the Good News came to them not in word only but in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance. And the Thessalonians became imitators of Paul and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction, with joy.

Their story had spread. They became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and Achaia, and the word of the Lord sounded out from them. People everywhere report how they “turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God”, and how they “wait for his Son from heaven”, whom God raised from the dead: Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

Paul writes with Silvanus and Timothy to the young church in Thessalonica, which Paul had visited (see Acts 17). It is usually dated around AD 50 or 51, and many scholars count it among the earliest writings of the New Testament. Tradition holds that Paul wrote it. Christians read the coming of the Son from heaven in different ways, and the later chapters of the letter say more about it.

Paul asks the Thessalonians to remember how he came to them. He had just been shamefully treated at Philippi, and still he and his companions grew bold to tell the Good News in much conflict. They did not flatter anyone. They did not ask for money or praise, though they might have claimed the weight of apostles. Instead they were gentle, “like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.” They worked night and day so that no one would be burdened, and they urged each person as a father does his own children.

Then the chapter turns hard. Paul thanks God that they received the message as God’s word, and he says they suffered from their own countrymen as the assemblies in Judea suffered. In that setting he speaks sharply of “the Jews” who killed Jesus and the prophets. The chapter ends in longing: he tried again and again to see them, and he calls them his hope, his joy and his glory.

Paul writes to a young assembly he had to leave soon after he helped found it, and he reminds them of how he and his co-workers behaved among them. The letter is usually dated around AD 50 to 51, which would make it one of the earliest New Testament writings. See Acts 17 for the visit. The sharp words in verses 14 to 16 come out of a conflict inside the Jewish world, and Paul was a Jew himself. They have been badly misused against Jewish people as a whole, and many readers take them to describe particular opponents.

Paul could not stand the waiting. Alone in Athens, he and his companions decided to send Timothy to the Thessalonians to strengthen them and comfort them in their faith. Paul feared that the tempter had tempted them and that all his work had been for nothing. He reminds them that he had told them beforehand that affliction would come.

Then comes the news he longed for. Timothy has just returned with glad word of their faith and love, and that they remember Paul with good memories and long to see him as he longs to see them. The relief breaks out in a single line: “For now we live, if you stand fast in the Lord.”

He cannot thank God enough. He prays night and day to see their faces again, and he asks the Lord to make them increase and overflow in love for one another and for all people.

This chapter is the emotional center of the letter. Paul is writing just after Timothy’s report, probably from Corinth, and the letter is usually dated around AD 50 to 51. He has been separated from the church by force of circumstances and by worry, and the letter answers a report that has set his mind at rest. See Acts 17 and Acts 18 for his journey. The prayer at the end leads into the practical teaching of the next chapter.

Paul urges the Thessalonians to keep walking in what they were taught about pleasing God. He speaks plainly about sexual conduct: they are to abstain from sexual immorality, to live in holiness and honor, and not to wrong a brother or sister in this matter. He praises their love for the believers across Macedonia and asks for more of it. He asks them to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands.

Then he turns to grief. Some of them have died, and the living are afraid for them. Paul does not want them to grieve like those who have no hope. Because Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in him. The Lord himself will descend with a shout and a trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up together with them. The chapter closes with a charge: “Therefore comfort one another with these words.”

A church that is barely a year or two old has already buried some of its own, and the question of what happens to them presses on the living. The letter is usually dated around AD 50 to 51. Christians differ on how to read the details of the Lord’s coming and being caught up in the clouds, including the order and timing of events. The teaching on sexual conduct and on daily work belongs to the same letter and reflects the everyday life of a new congregation in a Greek city. See also 1 Corinthians 15.

Paul has no need to write about times and seasons, because they already know that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. When people are saying, “Peace and safety,” sudden destruction comes, like birth pains on a pregnant woman. But the Thessalonians are not in darkness. They are children of light and of the day, so they are to stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God did not appoint them to wrath but to salvation, so that whether they wake or sleep they live together with Christ.

Then the letter speeds up. Respect those who labor among you. Be at peace. Admonish the disorderly, encourage the faint-hearted, support the weak. Never return evil for evil. “Always rejoice.” Pray without ceasing. Test all things and hold on to the good. A prayer for the whole person closes the letter.

Paul writes to a church under pressure, and the closing chapter gathers short instructions that could be read aloud in one sitting. He even commands that the letter be read to all the believers, which shows that these words were meant for the whole assembly. The letter is usually dated around AD 50 to 51. The picture of the day of the Lord as a thief draws on a theme also found in the teaching of Jesus, and Christians differ on how to read the timing of the end. See 2 Thessalonians 2 for what Paul writes next on this subject.
